# Problem 4.1 
Recall the peppered moth analysis introduced in Example 4.2. In the field, it is 
quite difficult to distinguish the insularia and typica phenotypes due to 
variations in wing color and mottle. In addition to the 622 moths mentioned in 
the example, suppose the sample collected by the researchers actually included 
$n_U=578$ more moths that were known to be insularia or typical but whose exact 
phenotypes could not be determined.

## a
Derive the EM algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation of $p_C, p_I, p_T$ for
this modified problem having observed data $n_C, n_I, n_T, n_U$ as given above.\
![]("C:/Users/jacma/OneDrive/school work/UMD/Stat 705 Computational Stats/HW Images/705 HW7 1a.jpg") 

## b
Apply the algorithm to find the MLEs.
```{r}
# n_C, n_I, n_T, n_U 
x <- c(85,196,341,578)
n <- rep(0,6)
p <- rep(1/3,3) # initial values
iter <- 50
base.values <- matrix(0,3,iter+1) # to save all results
# function to compute expectations
allele_estep <- function(x,p){
  # p: C I T,  x: C I T U
  # common factors
  A <- p[1]^2+2*p[1]*p[2]+2*p[1]*p[3]
  B <- p[2]^2+2*p[2]*p[3]
  C <- p[2]^2+2*p[2]*p[3]+p[3]^2
    
  # these are the same, since n_u is only I or T
  n.cc <- (x[1]*(p[1]^2))/A
  n.ci <- (2*x[1]*p[1]*p[2])/A
  n.ct <- (2*x[1]*p[1]*p[3])/A
  # these have extra uncertainty, additional terms are E[n_{}^u] 
  n.ii <- (x[2]*(p[2]^2))/B + (x[4]*p[2]^2)/C
  n.it <- (2*x[2]*p[2]*p[3])/B + (2*x[4]*p[2]*p[3])/C
  n.tt <- x[3] + (x[4]*(p[3]^2))/C
  n <- c(n.cc,n.ci,n.ct,n.ii,n.it,n.tt)
  return(n)
}

# function to maximize probabilities
allele_mstep <- function(x,n){
  p.c <- (2*n[1]+n[2]+n[3])/(2*sum(x))
  p.i <- (2*n[4]+n[5]+n[2])/(2*sum(x))
  p.t <- (2*n[6]+n[3]+n[5])/(2*sum(x))
  p <- c(p.c,p.i,p.t)
  return(p)
}

## EM Algorithm, repeat steps iter times
base_em_start <- Sys.time()
for(i in 2:iter){
  n <- allele_estep(x,p)
  p <- allele_mstep(x,n)
  base.values[,i] <- p
}
base_em_time <- Sys.time() - base_em_start
p
```

## c
Estimate the standard errors and pairwise correlations for 
$\hat{p_C},\hat{p_I},\hat{p_T}$ using SEM algorithm.
```{r}
# Uses allele_estep, allele_mstep
p <- rep(1/3,3) # reset initial values
p_update <- p
theta <- matrix(0,3,3)
psi <- rep(0,3)
r <- matrix(0,3,3)

for(i in 1:iter){
    n_update = allele_estep(x,p_update)
    p_update = allele_mstep(x,n_update)
}

# initialize theta
for(j in 1:length(p)){
  theta[,j] <- p_update
  theta[j,j] <- p[j]
}

# main algorithm
for(t in 1:5){
  n <- allele_estep(x,p)
  p.hat <- allele_mstep(x,n)
  for(j in 1:length(p)){
    theta[j,j] <- p.hat[j]
    n <- allele_estep(x,theta[,j])
    psi <- allele_mstep(x,n)
    for(i in 1:length(p)){r[i,j] <- (psi[i]-p_update[i])/(theta[j,j]-p_update[j])}
  }
  p <- p.hat
}

## COMPLETE INFORMATION
iy.hat<-matrix(0,2,2)
iy.hat[1,1] <- ((2*n_update[1]+n_update[2]+n_update[3])/(p_update[1]^2) +
     (2*n_update[6]+n_update[3]+n_update[5])/(p_update[3]^2))
iy.hat[2,2] <- ((2*n_update[4]+n_update[5]+n_update[2])/(p_update[2]^2) +
     (2*n_update[6]+n_update[3]+n_update[5])/(p_update[3]^2))
iy.hat[1,2] <- (2*n_update[6]+n_update[3]+n_update[5])/(p_update[3]^2)
iy.hat[2,1] <- iy.hat[1,2]

## COMPUTES STANDARD ERRORS AND CORRELATIONS
var.hat <- solve(iy.hat)%*%(diag(2)+t(r[-3,-3])%*%solve(diag(2)-t(r[-3,-3])))
sd.hat <- c(sqrt(var.hat[1,1]),sqrt(var.hat[2,2]),sqrt(sum(var.hat)))
cor.hat <- c(var.hat[1,2]/(sd.hat[1]*sd.hat[2]),
    (-var.hat[1,1]-var.hat[1,2])/(sd.hat[1]*sd.hat[3]),
    (-var.hat[2,2]-var.hat[1,2])/(sd.hat[2]*sd.hat[3]))
cat('Allele Proportions: p_C, p_I, p_T \n')
p
cat('Estimated Standard errors: p_C, p_I, p_T \n')
sd.hat
cat('Estimated Pairwise Correlations: (p_C,p_I), (p_C,p_T), (p_I,p_T) \n')
cor.hat 
```
The results above mean the proportions of the I and T alleles both have an error
of about 1.1%, while the C allele has an error of about 0.3%. Based on the 
calculated proportions, we can say that $C\in(3,3.9)$%, $I\in(20,23)$%,
$T\in(73,76)$%, all roughly speaking and based on our sample. These results can
vary with different runs of the code. \
The correlations are all negative, which is intuitive because the proportions
must all sum to one, so if any of them increase it is expected for the others
to decrease. The strongest correlations are with the T allele, which has a very
strong negative correlation with I. This means that if we see more and more T 
moths, we expect to see far fewer I moths. The other correlations are only 
slightly negative, but have a similar interpretation

## d
Estimate the standard errors and pairwise correlations for 
$\hat{p_C},\hat{p_I},\hat{p_T}$ by boot-strapping.
```{r}
# uses allele_estep, allele_mstep
p <- rep(1/3,3) # reset initial values
n <- rep(0,6)
boots <- 10000
theta <- matrix(0,3,boots)

## MAIN
for(i in 1:iter){
  n <- allele_estep(x,p)
  p <- allele_mstep(x,n)
}
theta[,1] <- p
for(j in 2:boots){
  # randomly generate initial group sizes
  n_c <- rbinom(1, sum(x), x[1]/sum(x))
  n_i <- rbinom(1, sum(x) - n_c, x[2]/(sum(x)-x[1]))
  n_t <- rbinom(1, sum(x) - n_c - n_i, x[3]/(sum(x)-x[1]-x[2]))
  n_u <- sum(x) - n_c - n_i - n_t
  x.new <- c(n_c,n_i,n_t,n_u)
  n <- rep(0,6)
  p <- rep(1/3,3)
  for(i in 1:iter){
    n <- allele_estep(x.new,p)
    p <- allele_mstep(x.new,n)
  }
  theta[,j] <- p
}

# compute bootstrapped sample std deviation and correlation
sd.hat <- c(sd(theta[1,]), sd(theta[2,]), sd(theta[3,]))
cor.hat <- c(cor(theta[1,],theta[2,]), cor(theta[1,],theta[3,]),
    cor(theta[2,],theta[3,]))

cat('Allele Proportions: p_C, p_I, p_T \n')
p
cat('Standard Error Estimates: p_C, p_I, p_T \n')
sd.hat
cat('Estimated Pairwise Correlations: (p_C,p_I), (p_C,p_T), (p_I,p_T) \n')
cor.hat
```
The results have very similar interpretations to part c).

## e
**I feel like I have the set-up correct, but this is getting an error I can't**
**seem to fix.** \
Implement the EM gradient algorithm for these data. Experiment with step-halving
to ensure ascent and with other step scalings that may speed up convergence.\
Derivation of algorithm is written in my notes.\
![]("C:/Users/jacma/OneDrive/school work/UMD/Stat 705 Computational Stats/HW Images/705 HW7 1e.jpg")
```{r,warning=FALSE}
# uses allele_estep, allele_mstep
p <- rep(1/3,3) # reset initial values
n <- rep(0,9)
gradient.values <- matrix(0,3,iter+1) # to save all results
gradient.values[,1] <- p
alpha.default <- 1

allele_estep2 <- function(x,p){
  # p: C I T,  x: C I T U
  # common factors
  A <- p[1]^2+2*p[1]*p[2]+2*p[1]*p[3]
  B <- p[2]^2+2*p[2]*p[3]
  C <- p[2]^2+2*p[2]*p[3]+p[3]^2
    
  # same as text
  n.cc <- (x[1]*(p[1]^2))/A
  n.ci <- (2*x[1]*p[1]*p[2])/A
  n.ct <- (2*x[1]*p[1]*p[3])/A
  n.ii <- (x[2]*(p[2]^2))/B 
  n.it <- (2*x[2]*p[2]*p[3])/B 
  n.tt <- x[3]
  # additional unknown group
  m.ii <- (x[4]*p[2]^2)/C
  m.it <- (2*x[4]*p[2]*p[3])/C
  m.tt <- (x[4]*(p[3]^2))/C
  n <- c(n.cc,n.ci,n.ct,n.ii,n.it,n.tt,m.ii,m.it,m.tt)
  return(n)
}
# compute log-likelihood, combine into four bins: C, I, T, U first three stay the same (?)
allele_log <- function(x,p){
  l <- x[1]*log(2*p[1] - p[1]^2) + 
    x[2]*log(p[2]^2 + 2*p[2]*p[3]) + 
    2*x[3]*log(p[3]) +
    x[4]*log(p[2]^2+2*p[2]*p[3]+p[3]^2)
  return(l)
}

# gradient of Q
Q.prime <- function(n,p){
  # first parts the same, plus additional terms
  dp_C <- (2*n[1]+n[2]+n[3])/(p[1]) - (n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3])
  dp_I <- (n[2]+2*n[4]+n[5]+2*n[7]+n[8])/(p[2]) - 
    (n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3])
  dQ <- c(dp_C,dp_I)
  return(dQ)
}

# Hessian of Q
Q.2prime <- function(n,p){
  dp_C2 <- -(2*n[1]+n[2]+n[3])/(p[1]^2) - (n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3]^2)
  dp_I2 <- (n[2]+2*n[4]+n[5]+2*n[7]+n[8])/(p[2]^2) - 
    (n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3]^2)
  dp_Cp_I <- -(n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3]^2)
  d2Q <- matrix(c(dp_C2,dp_Cp_I,dp_Cp_I,dp_I2), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
  return(d2Q)
}

## MAIN
l.old <- allele_log(x,p)
gradient_em_start <- Sys.time()
FIXED <- TRUE
if (FIXED){
  for(i in 1:iter){
    alpha <- alpha.default
    n <- allele_estep2(x,p)
    p.new <- p[1:2] - alpha*solve(Q.2prime(n,p))%*%Q.prime(n,p)
    p.new[3] <- 1 - p.new[1] - p.new[2]
    if((sum(p.new>0) == 3) && (sum(p.new<1)==3)){l.new <- allele_log(x,p.new)}
    while((sum(p.new>0) == 3)  || (sum(p.new<1)==3) || (l.new < l.old)){
      alpha <- alpha/2 # step halving
      p.new <- p[1:2] - alpha*solve(Q.2prime(n,p))%*%Q.prime(n,p)
      p.new[3] <- 1 - p.new[1] - p.new[2]
      if((sum(p.new>0) == 3) && (sum(p.new<1)==3)){l.new <- allele_log(x,p.new)}
      }
    p <- p.new
    gradient.values[,i+1] <- p
    l.old <- l.new
  }
  gradient_em_time <- Sys.time() - gradient_em_start
}
```

## f 
**Unsure about derivations, MANY places to make algebraic errors. Is also giving**

Implement Aitken accelerated EM for these data. Use step-halving. \
Derivation of stuff also on notes paper. \
![]("C:/Users/jacma/OneDrive/school work/UMD/Stat 705 Computational Stats/HW Images/705 HW7 1f.jpg")
```{r}
# uses allele_estep2, allele_mstep, allele_log
p <- rep(1/3,3) # reset initial values
n <- rep(0,9)
aitken.values <- matrix(0,3,iter+1) # to save all results
aitken.values[,1] <- p
alpha.default <- 2

# computes complete information, the negative expectation of 2nd deriv of Q
allele.iy <- function(n,p){
  iy.hat<-matrix(0,2,2)
  iy.hat[1,1] <- (2*n[1]+n[2]+n[3])/(p[1]^2) + 
    (n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3]^2)
  iy.hat[2,2] <- (n[2]+2*n[4]+n[5]+2*n[7]+n[8])/(p[2]^2) + 
    (n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3]^2)
  iy.hat[1,2] <- iy.hat[2,1] <- (n[3]+n[5]+2*n[6]+n[8]+2*n[9])/(p[3]^2)
  return(iy.hat)
}

# second derivative matrix for log-likelihood
allele_log_2prime <- function(x,p){
  l.2prime <- matrix(0,2,2)
  l.2prime[1,1] <- 2*x[1]/(p[1]^2+2*p[1]) - x[1]*(2*p[1]+2)^2/(p[1]^2+2*p[1])^2 -
    2*x[4]/(1-2*p[1]-p[1]^2) - x[4]*(-2*p[1]-2)^2/(1-2*p[1]-p[1]^2)^2 - 
    4*x[2]*p[2]^2/(2*p[2]-2*p[2]*p[1]-p[2]^2)^2 - 2*x[3]/(1-p[1]-p[2])^2
  l.2prime[2,2] <- -2*x[2]/(2*p[2]-2*p[1]*p[2]-p[1]^2) -
    x[2]*(2-2*p[2]-2*p[1])^2/(2*p[2]-2*p[1]*p[2]-p[2]^2)^2 -
    2*x[3]/(1-p[1]-p[2])^2
  l.2prime[1,2] <- l.2prime[2,1] <- 2*x[2]*p[2]*(2-2*p[1]-2*p[2])/
    (2*p[2]-2*p[1]*p[2]-p[2]^2)^2 -
    2*x[2]/(2*p[2]-2*p[1]*p[2]-p[2]^2) - 2*x[3]/(1-p[1]-p[2])^2
  return(l.2prime)
}

if (FIXED){
  l.old <- allele_log(x,p)
  aitken_em_start <- Sys.time()
  for(i in 1:iter){
    alpha <- alpha.default
    n <- allele_estep2(x,p)
    p.em <- allele_mstep(x,n)
    p.new <- (p[1:2] - alpha*solve(allele_log_2prime(x,p))%*%
                allele.iy(n,p)%*%(p.em[1:2]-p[1:2]))
    p.new[3] <- 1 - p.new[1] - p.new[2]
    if((sum(p.new>0) == 3) && (sum(p.new<1)==3)){l.new <- allele_log(x,p.new)}
    # REDUCE ALPHA UNTIL A CORRECT STEP IS REACHED
    while(sum(p.new>0) == 3 || (sum(p.new<1)==3) || l.new < l.old){
      alpha <- alpha/2
      p.new <- (p[1:2] - alpha*solve(allele_log_2prime(x,p))%*%
                  allele.iy(n,p)%*%(p.em[1:2]-p[1:2]))
      p.new[3] <- 1 - p.new[1] - p.new[2]
      if((sum(p.new>0) == 3) && (sum(p.new<1)==3)){l.new <- allele_log(x,p.new)}
    }
    p <- p.new
    aitken.values[,i+1] <- p
    l.old <- l.new
  }
  aitken_em_time <- Sys.time() - aitken_em_start
}
```

## g
Implement quasi-Newton EM for these data. Compare performance with and without 
step-halving. \
This uses everything that has been implemented previously, but with a different
algorithm.
```{r}
# uses allele_estep, allele_log, Q.prime, Q.2prime
p <- rep(1/3,3) # reset initial values
n <- rep(0,6)
m <- matrix(0,2,2)
b <- matrix(0,2,2)
qn.values <- matrix(0,3,iter+1)
qn.values[,1] <- p
alpha.default <- 2

if (FIXED) {
  l.old <- allele_log(x,p)
  qn_em_start <- Sys.time()
  for(i in 1:iter){
    alpha <- alpha.default
    n <- allele_estep2(x,p)
    m <- Q.2prime(n,p) - b
    p.new <- p[1:2] - alpha*solve(m)%*%Q.prime(n,p)
    p.new[3] <- 1 - p.new[1] - p.new[2]
    if((sum(p.new>0) == 3) && (sum(p.new<1)==3)){l.new <- allele_log(x,p.new)}
    # REDUCE ALPHA UNTIL A CORRECT STEP IS REACHED
    while((sum(p.new>0) == 3) || (sum(p.new<1)==3) || l.new < l.old){
      alpha <- alpha/2
      p.new <- p[1:2] - alpha*solve(m)%*%Q.prime(n,p)
      p.new[3] <- 1 - p.new[1] - p.new[2]
      if(p.new > 0 && p.new < 1){l.new <- allele_log(x,p.new)}}
      at <- p.new[1:2]-p[1:2]
      n <- allele_estep(x,p.new)
      bt <- Q.prime(n,p)-Q.prime(n,p.new)
      vt <- bt - b%*%at
      ct <- as.numeric(1/(t(vt)%*%at))
      b <- b + ct*vt%*%t(vt)
      p <- p.new
      qn.values[,i+1] <- p
      l.old <- l.new
  }
  qn_em_time <- Sys.time() - qn_em_start
  p
}
```

# Problem 4.2
$N=\sum_{i=1}^{16} n_i=1500$, with $n_i =$ number of respondents reporting $i=1,...,16$ \
Three groups: Zero (z), Typical (t), Promiscuous (p). \
$\alpha$: probability of belonging to Zero reporting 0 despite untrue.\
$\beta$: probability of belonging to Typical with typical behavior, $n_i \sim Poi(\mu)$ \
$1-\alpha-\beta$: probability of belonging to high risk Promiscuous group, 
respond truthfully, $n_i\sim Poi(\lambda)$ \

##  a
Show that the EM algorithm provides the following updates (written by hand):\
![]("C:/Users/jacma/OneDrive/school work/UMD/Stat 705 Computational Stats/HW Images/705 HW7 2a.jpg")

## b and c
Estimate the parameters of the model, using the observed data. \
Estimate the standard errors and pairwise correlations of your parameter 
estimates, using any available method.
```{r}
# function for probabilities
pi_i <- function(alpha,beta,mu,lambda,i) {
  if (i==0){alpha + beta * exp(-mu) + (1-alpha-beta)*exp(-lambda)}
  else {beta* mu^i* exp(-mu) + (1-alpha-beta)* lambda^i *exp(-lambda)}}

z_0 <- function(alpha,beta,mu,lambda,i) {
  alpha / pi_i(alpha, beta, mu, lambda,i)}

t_i <- function(alpha,beta,mu,lambda,i){
  beta * mu^i * exp(-mu)/pi_i(alpha, beta, mu, lambda,i)}

p_i <- function(alpha,beta,mu,lambda,i){
  (1-alpha-beta) * lambda^i * exp(-lambda)/pi_i(alpha, beta, mu, lambda,i)
}

# data, initial values
encounters <- 0:16
frequencies <- c(379,299,222,145,109,95,73,59,45,30,24,12,4,2,0,1,1)
alpha <- 0.5
beta <- 0.2
mu <- 2
lambda <- 5
estimate <- c(alpha, beta, mu, lambda)
iter <- 20
# bootstrapping variables for part c)
boots <- 1000
N <- sum(frequencies)
nullprob <- frequencies/N
for (i in 1:boots){
  freq <- rmultinom(1,size=N,prob=nullprob)
  # initial guesses
  alpha <- 0.5
  beta <- 0.2
  mu <- 2
  lambda <- 5
  j <- c(encounters)
  n_i <- freq
  for (i in 1:iter){
    alpha_t <- alpha
    beta_t <- beta
    mu_t <- mu
    lambda_t <- lambda
    # compute alpha update
    alpha_t1 <- n_i[1] * z_0(alpha_t,  beta_t, mu_t, lambda_t, j[1])/sum(n_i)
  
    # compute beta update
    b <- 0
    for (i in 1:length(j)){
      b <- b + n_i[i]*t_i(alpha_t,beta_t,mu_t,lambda_t,j[i])}
    beta_t1 <- b/sum(n_i)
  
    # compute mu update
    m <- 0
    for (i in 1:length(j)){
      m <- m + j[i]*n_i[i]*t_i(alpha_t,beta_t,mu_t,lambda_t,j[i])/b}
    mu_t1 <- m
  
    # compute lambda update
    p <- l <- 0
    for (i in 1:length(j))  {
      p <- p + n_i[i]*p_i(alpha_t,  beta_t, mu_t, lambda_t, j[i])}
    for (i in 1:length(j))  {
      l <- l + j[i]*n_i[i]*p_i(alpha_t,  beta_t, mu_t, lambda_t, j[i])/p}
    lambda_t1 <- l
  
    estimate <- rbind(estimate, c(alpha_t1,beta_t1,mu_t1,lambda_t1))
    # update parameters
    alpha <- alpha_t1
    beta <- beta_t1
    mu <- mu_t1
    lambda <- lambda_t1
  }
}
# b)
cat('Parameter Estimates: Alpha, Beta, Mu, Lambda \n')
estimate[1,]
# c)
cat('Corresponding Standard Errors: \n')
diag(cov(estimate))
cat('Pairwise Correlations: Alpha[1], Beta[2], Mu[3], Lambda[4] \n')
cor(estimate)
```
